title: Supporting Indigenous-Led Work on Long Island
summary: Ways to support Indigenous-led organizations and knowledge holders without creating unpaid labor or competing projects.
content:
Questions visitors ask

Open a question for a concise answer, context, and sources.

What are practical ways to support Indigenous-led work on Long Island today?

Support Indigenous-led work through the public channels each organization chooses: attend programs, buy directly from Native artists and businesses, donate to official campaigns, and share accurate information. Avoid inventing a project on a community's behalf or assuming that every organization can accept volunteers.

The most useful support follows priorities that Native-led organizations have made public. That may include buying work directly from Native artists, visiting open businesses and museums, attending public programs, donating through an official campaign, or amplifying an announced land, language, health, education, or preservation initiative. Check current information before giving because organizations and needs change. If no request for volunteers or professional help is posted, ask briefly and accept that the answer may be no. Direct support respects self-determination and avoids creating extra administrative work.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, pp. 6-7, 12, 15, 56-57, 60-63.
  • Gaynell Stone, The Shinnecock Indians: A Culture History (1983), pp. 338, 345.
How can someone donate, volunteer, or offer professional help without creating extra work for Native organizations?

Support organizations by prioritizing their publicly stated requests rather than offering unsolicited, self-directed help. Donate directly to established funds, respect organizational boundaries, pay Native professionals for their labor, and understand that some groups may lack the capacity to coordinate volunteers.

Respectful support of Indigenous-led organizations requires non-Native volunteers and donors to prioritize the self-stated needs of the community rather than imposing unsolicited projects. In 'We Are Still Here!' (1998), John A. Strong emphasizes that direct, unconditional financial donations to established institutions—such as the Shinnecock Cultural Center and Museum or the Unkechaug Cultural School—are the most effective way to assist, as they respect tribal autonomy and do not drain limited administrative labor (p. 7). Well-meaning individuals often offer professional services or volunteer labor that requires intensive coordination, creating additional work for small, understaffed tribal offices. For contemporary initiatives like Ma's House & BIPOC Art Studio, founder Jeremy Dennis provides clear, public channels for donations, programming registries, and wish lists to streamline community support (createspace, p. 295). Donors should always fund existing, Native-designed initiatives rather than creating separate projects. Furthermore, any professional collaboration must involve fair financial compensation for Native consultants and elders, honoring their intellectual property and sovereign expertise rather than expecting free educational labor.

Sources

  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, p. 7.
  • Beverly Jensen, Shinnecock Indian Nation (2015), p. 85.
How can non-Native people ask questions without expecting Native people to do unpaid educational labor?

Non-Native people can avoid exploiting Native communities by consulting existing public records, books, and museum materials first. When direct inquiry is necessary, seek formal consent, treat consultations as professional services, pay Native experts fairly, and respect communal boundaries.

To engage respectfully, non-Native learners must recognize that Indigenous people are not public libraries or automatic educational resources. Expecting Native scholars, elders, or community members to answer uninvited historical or cultural questions constitutes a form of extraction and unpaid labor. This exploitative dynamic mirrors deep historical inequalities, such as those faced by Samson Occom, who was paid half the salary of his white missionary colleagues while performing the exhausting dual work of a schoolmaster and minister. Before seeking individual consultation, researchers should exhaustively study the substantial, pre-existing literature compiled by both professional scholars and tribal organizations. When a project requires direct tribal input, researchers must approach tribal historic preservation officers (THPOs) or tribal councils formally. Seek explicit, consent-based agreements, define clear boundaries, and establish professional compensation terms. If a Native expert, elder, or artist provides expertise, they must be formally credited and paid standard consulting fees—treating their intellectual and cultural knowledge as a professional asset. Finally, if a tribal representative or organization declines to participate or sets boundaries on what knowledge is shared, non-Native researchers must accept and respect that decision without pushback.

Sources

  • Samson Occom; edited by Joanna Brooks, Joanna Brooks, ed., The Collected Writings of Samson Occom, Mohegan, pp. 5, 54-55.
  • John A. Strong, The Montaukett Indians of Eastern Long Island (2001), pp. xiii, 184.
  • John A. Strong, We Are Still Here, pp. 6-7.
  • John A. Strong, America's Early Whalemen, pp. Acknowledgments, 115.
why_this_matters: Respectful public learning depends on clear answers, transparent sources, and attention to the authority and privacy of living Indigenous communities.
